title: Tenant‑prioritized slew controller with safe fallbacks
creator: Sofia Martinez
description: Implement a new autoscaling policy engine component (Slew Controller) that enforces tenant‑weighted scaling targets, limits slew (rate of capacity change), and provides deterministic safe fallbacks when capacity or kernels are constrained. This ticket covers policy specification, control algorithm, safety envelope, integration tests, and runtime telemetry.
background: Current autoscalers either aggressively chase throughput or conservatively allocate headroom. We need a mid‑path controller that: 1) honors per‑tenant throughput guarantees (committed SLAs), 2) smooths scale actions to avoid oscillation, 3) exposes a predictable fallback path that downgrades throughput tiers before failing requests, and 4) is compatible with Dedicated fleet capacity contracts and cache affinity constraints.
goals: Define a target metric composition (weighted throughput + p95 latency + queue depth) for tenant sizing
Design and implement a proportional‑integral (PI) based slew controller with rate limits and budget accounting
Implement deterministic safe fallback behavior under constrained capacity: graceful degradation → prioritized shedding → fallback model variant routing
Ship unit, integration, and chaos tests validating non‑oscillation, tenant fairness, and SLA preservation under spike patterns
Add telemetry dashboards and cost/regression alerts to the Console
success_metrics: p95 request latency degradation under 10% vs baseline during 3x short spikes
No more than 2 unnecessary scale events per 30 minutes for steady workloads
Committed SLA violations reduced to <0.1% over a 7‑day stress test
Scaling-related cost delta within budget envelope (<= +5% for tail events)
acceptance_criteria: Policy spec document reviewed and approved by Runtime and Fleet teams (link in links)
Implementation passes autotests: unit PI controller tests, integration against autoscale simulator, and canary on staging
When capacity is exhausted, controller transitions through fallback states (graceful degrade, tenant shed, model fallback) in documented order
Controller emits the following telemetry at 1s cadence: target_capacity, requested_scale_steps, applied_scale, headroom_credit, fallback_state
Regression alert fires if controller oscillates (scale up followed by full scale down) more than 3 times within 15 minutes
design_decisions: Use a PI controller as the baseline: proportional term for fast reaction to throughput delta, integral term with anti‑windup for persistent error
Compose target metric as weighted sum: committed_throughput * tenant_weight + alpha * p95_latency_margin + beta * normalized_queue_depth
Slew limit is enforced on applied capacity (max X GPUs/minute per fleet); implement both absolute and relative limits
Headroom credits are debited on speculative scale requests and reconciled over time; credits prevent repeated speculative spikes
Fallback hierarchy: (1) reduce burst headroom for low‑priority tenants, (2) enforce per‑tenant rate caps, (3) route to lower‑throughput model variant or lower‑precision quantized model
Make fallback policies declarative and pluggable so Console and PM can configure tenant priorities without code changes
tradeoffs: Conservative slew reduces oscillation but increases latency when sudden demand surges — mitigated via brief predictive warmups for forecasted bursts
Per‑tenant weighting favors SLA customers at cost of best‑effort workloads; requires clear billing/commitment mapping
Headroom credits add bookkeeping complexity and edge cases on long‑running sustained load; we keep a capped credit window to bound state size
implementation_plan: 1) Draft policy spec and parameter defaults (this ticket)
2) Implement PI controller library with anti‑windup and slew limiter in runtime repo (PR: link in links)
3) Add headroom credit ledger and per‑tenant weight store (db migration + admin API)
4) Integration: connect controller outputs to fleet allocator and kernel scheduler with safe dry‑run mode
5) Tests: unit + autoscale simulator scenarios + chaos (node flaps, kernel OOM) on staging
6) Canary rollout: 10% of Dedicated fleets with monitoring and automatic rollback
7) Post‑canary: iterate on defaults and expose tuning knobs in Console
